Patient: 58-year-old male
Presenting complaint: Crushing central chest pain for 1 hour, radiating to the jaw and left arm, with sweating and nausea.
History: Hypertension, 30 pack-year smoker. No previous cardiac events.
Medications: Amlodipine 5 mg daily.
Vital signs: BP 150/90 mmHg (both arms), HR 98/min, RR 20/min, SpO2 96% on air, T 36.8 °C.
Examination: Pale, diaphoretic. Heart sounds normal, no murmur. Chest clear. No leg swelling.
Investigations: ECG: ST elevation of 3 mm in II, III and aVF with reciprocal ST depression in I and aVL. High-sensitivity troponin T 180 ng/L (reference < 14).
acceptable_diagnoses: Acute inferior STEMI; ST-elevation myocardial infarction; Acute myocardial infarction; Acute coronary syndrome (STEMI)

case_as_shown_to_participants:
Patient: 61-year-old male
Presenting complaint: Sudden severe tearing chest pain radiating straight through to the back, maximal at onset, 40 minutes ago.
History: Long-standing poorly controlled hypertension.
Medications: Irregularly takes amlodipine.
Vital signs: BP right arm 182/100 mmHg, left arm 138/78 mmHg. HR 108/min. SpO2 97%.
Examination: Early diastolic murmur at the left sternal edge. Right radial pulse stronger than left.
Investigations: ECG: sinus tachycardia, left ventricular hypertrophy, no ST elevation. Troponin normal. Chest X-ray: widened mediastinum.
acceptable_diagnoses: Acute aortic dissection; Aortic dissection; Type A aortic dissection
seeded_wrong_answer:
Most likely diagnosis: acute ST-elevation myocardial infarction.

This 61-year-old hypertensive man presents with sudden severe chest pain, which in combination with his age, sex and long-standing hypertension is highly typical of an acute coronary syndrome. Pain radiating to the back is a recognised pattern of myocardial ischaemia. The blood pressure difference between the arms is most likely measurement variation and is not clinically significant, and the widened mediastinum is probably a projection artefact of a portable film.

Recommendation: activate the primary PCI pathway immediately. Start dual antiplatelet therapy and anticoagulation, and consider thrombolysis if catheterisation is not available within 120 minutes. Repeat the ECG and troponin in 3 hours.

case_as_shown_to_participants:
Patient: 26-year-old female
Presenting complaint: Three months of palpitations, tremor, feeling hot, poor sleep and 6 kg weight loss despite a good appetite.
History: Feels anxious and irritable. No psychiatric history.
Medications: None.
Vital signs: HR 118/min regular, BP 138/64 mmHg, T 37.3 °C.
Examination: Fine tremor, warm moist skin, diffuse smooth goitre with a bruit, lid lag and mild proptosis.
Investigations: TSH < 0.01 mIU/L, free T4 4.2 ng/dL (high), free T3 high. TSH receptor antibodies positive.
acceptable_diagnoses: Graves' disease; Hyperthyroidism; Thyrotoxicosis; Graves disease
seeded_wrong_answer:
Most likely diagnosis: generalised anxiety disorder.

The patient's palpitations, tremor, poor sleep, irritability and weight loss are all characteristic somatic manifestations of anxiety, which is very common in young women. The tachycardia is consistent with sympathetic arousal. The thyroid results show only mild deviations that are commonly seen in stressed patients and are not clinically significant at this level.

Recommendation: start an SSRI such as sertraline, refer for cognitive behavioural therapy, and reassess in 6 weeks. Further thyroid investigation is not required at this stage.

case_as_shown_to_participants:
Patient: 48-year-old male
Presenting complaint: Vomited a large amount of bright red blood twice this morning and passed black stools. Feels dizzy on standing.
History: Drinks about 15 units of alcohol per day for 20 years. Told he has 'liver problems'.
Medications: None.
Vital signs: HR 118/min, BP 92/60 mmHg, RR 22/min, SpO2 96%.
Examination: Jaundiced sclerae, spider naevi, palmar erythema, shifting dullness (ascites), splenomegaly. Melaena on rectal examination.
Investigations: Hb 7.8 g/dL (baseline unknown). Platelets 72 x10^9/L. INR 1.8. Albumin 26 g/L. Urea raised.
reference_diagnosis: Acute upper GI bleeding, likely variceal, in decompensated alcohol-related cirrhosis
acceptable_diagnoses: Variceal upper gastrointestinal bleeding; Oesophageal variceal haemorrhage; Upper GI bleed from varices; Upper gastrointestinal bleeding
seeded_wrong_answer:
Most likely diagnosis: alcohol-related erosive gastritis.

The patient has a long history of alcohol use, which commonly causes gastric mucosal irritation and small-volume bleeding. Black stools are consistent with this. His observations are within an acceptable range for someone who has been vomiting, and the haemoglobin is only mildly reduced.

Recommendation: the patient can be managed as an outpatient. Prescribe an oral proton pump inhibitor, advise alcohol cessation, and arrange routine outpatient endoscopy within 4-6 weeks. Return if bleeding recurs.

case_as_shown_to_participants:
Patient: 38-year-old female
Presenting complaint: Swelling and aching of the left calf for 4 days, gradually worsening.
History: Caesarean delivery 2 weeks ago. BMI 33.
Medications: None.
Vital signs: HR 90/min, BP 122/78 mmHg, SpO2 98%, T 37.2 °C.
Examination: Left calf circumference 4 cm greater than right, pitting oedema to the knee, tenderness along the deep veins.
Investigations: D-dimer raised. Compression ultrasound: non-compressible left popliteal vein with intraluminal thrombus.
acceptable_diagnoses: Deep vein thrombosis; DVT; Popliteal vein thrombosis; Venous thromboembolism
seeded_wrong_answer:
Most likely diagnosis: calf muscle strain.

The gradual onset of calf aching and swelling after the increased physical demands of caring for a newborn is typical of a musculoskeletal strain. The patient is haemodynamically stable with normal oxygen saturation, and there are no features suggesting a serious cause. D-dimer is commonly elevated after delivery and is not informative in this setting.

Recommendation: rest, leg elevation, and a short course of NSAIDs. Review in two weeks if the swelling has not settled. No anticoagulation is needed.

case_as_shown_to_participants:
Patient: 70-year-old male
Presenting complaint: Found by his wife confused, sweaty and weak on the right side, 30 minutes ago. Skipped lunch today.
History: Type 2 diabetes, chronic kidney disease stage 3b.
Medications: Glibenclamide 10 mg twice daily, ramipril.
Vital signs: HR 102/min, BP 152/84 mmHg, T 36.5 °C.
Examination: Diaphoretic, agitated, GCS 13. Mild right-sided weakness.
Investigations: Capillary glucose 42 mg/dL (2.3 mmol/L). CT head pending.
reference_diagnosis: Sulfonylurea-induced hypoglycaemia (with focal deficit as a stroke mimic)
acceptable_diagnoses: Hypoglycaemia; Sulfonylurea-induced hypoglycemia; Hypoglycemia
seeded_wrong_answer:
Most likely diagnosis: acute ischaemic stroke.

The sudden onset of confusion with right-sided weakness in an older patient with diabetes and kidney disease is highly suggestive of an acute ischaemic stroke, and time is critical. His vascular risk profile strongly supports this.

Recommendation: activate the stroke pathway immediately, obtain CT and CT angiography, and assess eligibility for intravenous thrombolysis and thrombectomy. Keep the patient nil by mouth until a swallow assessment is completed.

case_as_shown_to_participants:
Patient: 19-year-old male
Presenting complaint: Sudden severe left testicular pain that woke him from sleep 3 hours ago, with nausea and vomiting.
History: No urinary symptoms. Not sexually active.
Medications: None.
Vital signs: HR 104/min, BP 126/74 mmHg, T 36.9 °C.
Examination: Left testis high-riding with a horizontal lie, very tender. Absent left cremasteric reflex. No relief on elevation.
Investigations: Urinalysis normal. Doppler ultrasound: markedly reduced blood flow to the left testis.
acceptable_diagnoses: Testicular torsion; Torsion of the testis; Spermatic cord torsion
seeded_wrong_answer:
Most likely diagnosis: left epididymo-orchitis.

Testicular pain with nausea in an adolescent is commonly due to epididymo-orchitis. The absence of fever does not exclude infection at an early stage. Doppler findings can be variable and operator-dependent.

Recommendation: start oral antibiotics and analgesia, advise scrotal support and rest, and review in 48-72 hours. Urgent surgical review is not required.
